title: Heavy Metal Pollution to Shallow Groundwater Aquifer Caused by CO2 Leakage During Geological Carbon Storage (GCS)
content:
Abstract

In the context of geological carbon storage, assessing the geochemical alteration of groundwater in shallow aquifers due to unintended CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ leakage from deep CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ reservoirs is crucial. Elevated CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ levels can cause groundwater acidification and potential release of heavy metal from the aquifer rock to groundwater. In this study, we aim to elucidate the mechanism behind heavy metal release and discuss the selection of geochemical markers for detecting CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ leakage in aquifers with varying geochemical and hydrogeological characteristics. Reactive transport simulations were conducted using a Matlab reservoir simulation toolbox, which was validated against a field test for CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ leakage. Results indicate that while carbonate-rich aquifers exhibit a continuous release of heavy metals governed by rapidly dissolving impure carbonates, carbonate-poor aquifers show a more pronounced concentration shift of heavy metals controlled by surface complexation processes. Nevertheless, we find that dissolved inorganic carbon and pH can be used as general geochemical indicators for CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ exposure, regardless of the carbonate content in the aquifer rock. Most of the selected elements exceed or approach the maximum admissible levels for drinking water following the intrusion of CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$-rich water. Upon detection and cessation of the leakage source, all elements in the affected area revert to their initial levels under the natural flushing of groundwater flow, with the rate of self-remediation increasing in response to the hydraulic gradient.
